dataquality.q: A column has a value in every row, but 30% of those values are empty strings. Which dimension is really failing?
options: Timeliness
Uniqueness
Completeness
Consistency
dataquality.why: Empty strings are missing values in disguise, so completeness is low even though a null count shows zero. Always count blanks as well as nulls.

dataquality.q: What is blocking in entity resolution?
options: Stopping a load when a check fails
Only comparing records that share a cheap feature, like postcode
Hiding personal data from reviewers
Deleting records that score below the threshold
dataquality.why: Blocking cuts the number of pairs to compare. Without it, two lists of 50,000 names mean 2.5 billion comparisons.

dataquality.q: A migration finished. Row counts match exactly. The finance director asks if the data is right. What should you check next?
options: Nothing more, matching counts prove it
Control totals and per-row checksums
Only the first 10 rows by eye
Whether the table has an index
dataquality.why: Counts can match while values are wrong. Control totals catch wrong amounts in aggregate and checksums find the exact rows that differ.

dataquality.q: A daily CRM file breaks your pipeline every few weeks because columns get renamed. What is the lasting fix?
options: Rename the columns back by hand each time
Stop using the CRM file
Agree a data contract with a change notice period
Load every column as text so nothing fails
dataquality.why: A contract with the owning team moves the fix to the source and gives you notice before changes. Hand fixes repeat forever.

dataquality.q: A teammate sets one fuzzy-match threshold of 80 and auto-merges everything above it with no review. What is the main risk?
options: Different companies with similar names get merged
Matching will run too slowly
Exact duplicates will be missed
The score will go above 100
dataquality.why: At 80, names like 'Kestrel Dental' and 'Kestrel Motors' can merge wrongly. A review band between a low and a high threshold catches these.

spreadsheets.q: Which pandas operation is the code equivalent of an Excel XLOOKUP?
options: groupby with sum
A left merge on the lookup key
drop_duplicates
concat of two tables
spreadsheets.why: XLOOKUP finds a matching key in another table and brings back a value, which is exactly what a left join does.

spreadsheets.q: Why write the number 2400 with a currency number format instead of the text '£2,400'?
options: Text files are smaller
Excel cannot display text in bold
Users can still sort, filter and sum a real number
Number formats hide the value from users
spreadsheets.why: A number format only changes the display. Text that looks like money breaks sums and sorting, so users end up retyping it.

spreadsheets.q: Your script's weekly total is higher than the customer's. The workbook has a hidden row. What is the likely cause?
options: A hidden TOTAL row was read and added again
pandas skips hidden rows by default
Merged cells doubled every value
The file was saved in the wrong time zone
spreadsheets.why: Hidden rows are still in the file and pandas reads them. A hidden total row gets counted as if it were another record.

spreadsheets.q: A customer wants a VBA macro replaced by a script. What should happen before the macro is switched off?
options: Delete the macro so nobody runs both
Rewrite the report in a new BI tool
Ask IT to block all macros first
Run both on the same inputs and compare outputs
spreadsheets.why: A parallel run proves the script gives the same results, and often finds hidden bugs in the macro, before the owner signs off.

spreadsheets.q: Three receptionists edit one booking sheet and double-bookings keep happening. What is the strongest fix?
options: Add a colour rule that turns clashes red
Move bookings to a database with a UNIQUE (room, start) rule
Split the sheet into one tab per person
Email the sheet around instead of sharing it
spreadsheets.why: A database constraint rejects the clash on every write. Colour rules and data validation only warn, and users can paste over them.

webauto.q: A portal shows a table of orders. What should you check before writing a Playwright script to read it?
options: Whether the page runs on Linux
Whether the table loads from a JSON call in the Network tab
Whether the table has more than 100 rows
Whether the site uses a dark theme
webauto.why: If the page fetches its data as JSON, you can call that directly: faster, cleaner and less likely to break than clicking through the page.

webauto.q: Which Playwright locator is most likely to survive a redesign of the page?
options: locator('div > div:nth-child(3) > button')
locator('xpath=/html/body/div[2]/form/button')
get_by_role('button', name='Sign in')
locator('.btn-7f3a')
webauto.why: Role and visible name describe what a person sees, which rarely changes; positions and generated class names change with every layout tweak.

webauto.q: Your scraper reads a blank weight cell. What should it store?
options: None, a missing value
The previous row's weight
The text 'blank'
webauto.why: A blank means unknown. Storing 0 would quietly make totals and averages wrong.

webauto.q: The portal requires MFA and the job must run nightly. Which is the acceptable approach?
options: Use a clerk's login and SMS code sent to your phone
Retry the login until MFA is skipped
Use a CAPTCHA-solving service
A service account agreed with the security team, or a reused session a person renews
webauto.why: MFA is there to prove a person is present. Work with the customer's security team instead of around the control.

webauto.q: When is a browser agent a better fit than a Playwright script?
options: A daily download from the same page
A rare task where every site's form is different, checked by a person
Any task where speed matters most
Any job that must give identical results every run
webauto.why: Agents cope with varied, unfamiliar pages but are slower, cost more per run and vary between runs, so they suit the rare, varied long tail.

typescript.q: Which file should you commit so teammates install exactly the same package versions?
options: node_modules
tsconfig.json
.env
package-lock.json
typescript.why: The lockfile records exact versions. node_modules is rebuilt from it and should never be committed.

typescript.q: A handler does const body: Order = JSON.parse(raw). Why is this not safe?
options: JSON.parse is slow
Types are erased at runtime, so nothing checks that raw is really an Order
Order must be an interface, not a type
JSON.parse only works in the browser
typescript.why: The annotation only tells the compiler what to assume. Validate the parsed value with a schema such as zod before using it.

typescript.q: Three independent API calls take about 300 ms each. How do you make the total close to 300 ms?
options: Start all three and await Promise.all
Await each call in turn
Use setTimeout around each call
Put each call in its own try/catch
typescript.why: Promise.all runs the calls at the same time, so the total is about the slowest call instead of the sum.

typescript.q: Where should the code that calls the LLM API with your API key run?
options: In the browser, to save server costs
In a React component
On a server, reading the key from an environment variable
In a public GitHub Action log
typescript.why: Anything in browser code can be read in developer tools. Keep the key and the model call on the server.

typescript.q: tsc says: Type 'number | null' is not assignable to type 'number'. What is the best fix?
options: Add // @ts-ignore above the line
Handle the null case before using the value
Cast the value with as any
Turn off strict mode
typescript.why: The function can return null. Checking for it fixes the real bug; ignoring or casting only hides it.
